Paul and those with him put out to sea from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. But John left them there and went back to Jerusalem. They went on from Perga and arrived at Antioch near Pisidia. On the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and took their seats. When the Law and the Prophets had been read, the leaders of the synagogue sent a message to them: “Brothers, if one of you has a word of encouragement for the people, speak.” Paul stood up, waved his hand for quiet, and said, “People of Israel, and you God-fearing Gentiles, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our ancestors. During their stay as foreigners in the land of Egypt he made the people great, and with a raised arm he led them out of that land. For about forty years he bore with their ways in the desert, and after he had destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave their land to his people to possess. The whole span was about 450 years. After that he gave them judges until the time of the prophet Samuel. Next they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin, who reigned forty years. When he had set Saul aside, he raised up David to be their king, and he gave this testimony about him: ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man in tune with my heart, who will carry out all that I want.’ From this man’s line God has brought Israel a Savior, Jesus, just as he promised. Before Jesus came, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. As John was finishing his course, he kept saying, ‘Who do you think I am? I am not the one. No, someone is coming after me, and I am not fit to untie the sandal on his feet.’

Brothers and sisters, children of Abraham’s family, and you among us who fear God: this message of salvation has been sent out to us. The people of Jerusalem and their leaders did not know who he was, and they did not understand the words of the prophets that are read out every Sabbath; yet by condemning him they made those words come true. They found no charge that deserved death, and still they demanded that Pilate have him killed. When they had done everything that was written about him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now his witnesses to the people. And we are bringing you good news: the promise made to the ancestors God has now fulfilled for our children by raising up Jesus. So it stands written in the second psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ And that God raised him from the dead, never again to go back to decay, he declared in these words: ‘I will give you the holy blessings of David, the ones that can be trusted.’ That is why he also says in another psalm, ‘You will not let your Holy One undergo decay.’ For David, after serving God’s purpose in his own generation, fell asleep in death; he was laid to rest with his ancestors, and his body decayed. But the one whom God raised up did not undergo decay. So, brothers and sisters, you must know this: through this man forgiveness of sins is being announced to you, and from everything the law of Moses could not acquit you of, everyone who believes is acquitted through him. So be careful, or what was said in the Prophets may come upon you: ‘See, you who scorn, be astonished and vanish! For I am doing a work in your days, a work you would never believe, even if someone explained it to you.’”

As Paul and Barnabas were going out, the people kept urging them to speak about these things again on the next Sabbath. After the gathering broke up, many Jews and converts who worshiped God went along with Paul and Barnabas, who talked with them and kept persuading them to remain in the grace of God.

The whole city gathers to hear

The following Sabbath nearly the entire city came together to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, jealousy filled them, and they spoke against what Paul was saying and reviled him. Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly: “The word of God had to be spoken to you first. Since you push it away and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, see, we are turning to the Gentiles. For this is the command the Lord has given us: ‘I have set you as a light for the nations, so that you may be the means of salvation to the farthest part of the earth.’” When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and all who had been appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord spread across the whole region. But the Jews stirred up the respected women who worshiped God and the leading men of the city; they started a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their district. So the two shook the dust from their feet against them and went on to Iconium. And the disciples went on being filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.

fields.title: Acts 14
fields.body_html:
In Iconium

In Iconium the two of them went together into the synagogue of the Jews. They spoke in such a way that a large crowd of Jews and Greeks believed. But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and turned their minds against the brothers and sisters. So they stayed there a long time and spoke boldly, relying on the Lord. He bore witness to the word of his grace by allowing signs and wonders to happen through their hands. The people of the city were split: some sided with the Jews, and others with the apostles. When Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, set out to abuse the apostles and stone them, the apostles learned of it and escaped to Lystra and Derbe, towns of Lycaonia, and to the country around them. There they kept on proclaiming the gospel.

Called gods at Lystra

At Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He had been lame since birth and had never taken a step. The man was listening while Paul spoke. Paul fixed his eyes on him and saw that he had faith that he would be made well. So he said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet!” And the man leaped up and walked. When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices in the Lycaonian language: “The gods have become like humans and come down to us!” They began calling Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because Paul was the one who took the lead in speaking. Zeus had a temple just in front of the city. His priest came to the gates with bulls and garlands, for he and the crowds meant to offer sacrifice. But the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it. They ripped their garments and dashed into the middle of the crowd, crying out, “People, why are you doing these things? We are mortals with the same nature as you. We have come with the gospel, calling you to turn away from these empty things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything that is in them. In past generations he allowed every nation to walk in its own ways. Even so, he has not left himself without a witness. He does you good: he gives you rain from the sky and seasons that bear fruit, and he fills you with food and your hearts with gladness.” Saying these things, they could hardly hold the crowds back from offering sacrifice to them.

Paul stoned at Lystra

But Jews from Antioch and Iconium came on the scene and persuaded the crowds. They stoned Paul and hauled him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples stood in a circle around him, he rose and went back into the city. The next day he set out with Barnabas for Derbe.

Back through the cities, and home to Antioch

They proclaimed the gospel in that city and made many disciples. After that they retraced their steps to Lystra, to Iconium and to Antioch. They made the disciples strong in spirit and urged them to hold on to the faith, saying, “We must enter the kingdom of God by way of many afflictions.” In each church they appointed elders for the believers, and after praying and fasting, they placed them in the care of the Lord in whom they had believed. They crossed Pisidia and came into Pamphylia, and when they had spoken the word in Perga they went down to Attalia. From there they set sail for Antioch, the place where they had first been entrusted to God’s grace for the task that they had now carried out to the end. Once they had arrived, they called the church together and told all that God had done as he worked along with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained a long while with the disciples there.

fields.title: Acts 15
fields.body_html:
The question of circumcision

Some people came down from Judea and began teaching the brothers and sisters, “Unless you are circumcised as the custom of Moses requires, there is no way for you to be saved.” This led to fierce dispute and argument between them and Paul and Barnabas. So it was arranged that Paul and Barnabas and some others from among them should go up to Jerusalem and put this question to the apostles and the elders. The church sent them off, and as they went through Phoenicia and Samaria they told in full how the Gentiles were turning to God. The news brought great joy to all the brothers and sisters. On reaching Jerusalem they were received by the church, the apostles and the elders, and they told them everything God had done in company with them. Then some from the party of the Pharisees who had believed stood up and insisted, “These Gentiles have to be circumcised, and they must be ordered to keep the law of Moses.”

The apostles and the elders consider the matter

The apostles and the elders came together to consider this matter. After a long debate, Peter rose and spoke to them: “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made his choice among you: through my mouth the Gentiles were to hear the message of the gospel and come to believe. God, who knows every heart, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit, as he did for us as well. He made no difference at all between us and them, for he cleansed their hearts by faith. So why are you now putting God to the test? You would lay on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we ourselves have had the strength to carry. No, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, and they are saved in just the same way.”

The whole gathering grew quiet. Everyone listened to Barnabas and Paul as they told of the signs and wonders God had worked among the Gentiles through them. When they had finished, James responded, “Brothers, listen to what I have to say. Simeon has explained how God first looked with favor on the Gentiles, to take from among them a people to bear his name. What the prophets said agrees with this, as it stands written: ‘After this I will come back, and I will build again the fallen tent of David. I will build again its ruins and raise it up once more, so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, all the nations that are called by my name, says the Lord, who does these things, things made known long ago.’ So my judgment is that we should not make things hard for the Gentiles who are turning to God. Instead we should write to them that they keep away from what idols have defiled, from sexual immorality, from what has been strangled, and from blood. For Moses has been preached in every town since generations long past, and he is read aloud in the synagogues every Sabbath.”

A letter to the Gentile believers

Then the apostles and the elders, together with the whole church, decided to pick men from among themselves and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They chose Judas, known as Barsabbas, and Silas, men who held leading places among the brothers and sisters. They sent with them this letter: “From the apostles and the elders, your brothers, to the brothers and sisters of Gentile birth in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia: greetings. We have heard that some who went out from us have disturbed you with what they said and left you unsettled, though we gave them no such instructions. So we have come to one mind and decided to choose men and send them to you with Barnabas and Paul, whom we love, men who have given their lives over for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. So we are sending Judas and Silas, who will tell you the same things in person. The Holy Spirit and we ourselves have decided to place on you no burden beyond these essentials: keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you guard yourselves against these, you will be doing what is right. Farewell.”

So the men were sent on their way and went down to Antioch. There they called the whole community together and handed over the letter. When they had read it, they were glad for the encouragement it brought. Judas and Silas, who were also prophets, spoke at length to encourage the brothers and sisters and to make them strong. After they had stayed there for some time, the brothers and sisters let them go in peace, back to those who had sent them. Paul and Barnabas, though, stayed on in Antioch. Along with many others, they taught the word of the Lord and proclaimed it as good news.

Paul and Barnabas go separate ways

Some days later Paul said to Barnabas, “Come, let us go back and look in on the brothers and sisters in every town where we announced the word of the Lord, and find out how they are doing.” Barnabas wanted to bring John, also called Mark, with them too. But Paul did not think it right to take with them a man who had left them in Pamphylia and had not gone on with them to the work. The quarrel grew so heated that the two of them parted ways. Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to Cyprus, while Paul picked Silas and set out, after the brothers and sisters had commended him to the grace of the Lord. He traveled through Syria and Cilicia, making the churches strong.

fields.title: Acts 16
fields.body_html:
Timothy joins Paul and Silas

Paul came to Derbe and then on to Lystra. A disciple called Timothy was living there. His mother was a Jewish woman who believed, but his father was a Greek. The brothers and sisters in Lystra and Iconium thought highly of him. Paul wanted to have Timothy with him when he set out. With the Jews of that area in mind, he took him and circumcised him, since all of them knew that his father was a Greek. As they made their way from town to town, they passed on to the believers the decisions reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to observe. So the churches grew firmer in the faith, and their numbers rose day by day.

The call from Macedonia

They went on through the Phrygian and Galatian country, because the Holy Spirit had stopped them from speaking the word in Asia. Coming as far as Mysia, they made an attempt to go on into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit it. So they skirted Mysia and went down to Troas. In the night Paul saw a vision. A man of Macedonia stood there and pleaded with him, “Cross over to Macedonia and help us!” As soon as he had seen the vision, we looked for a way to set out for Macedonia, sure now that God had called us to bring the gospel to its people.

Lydia at the place of prayer

So we set sail from Troas and ran with a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day reached Neapolis. From there we made our way to Philippi, which ranks as a leading city of its district of Macedonia and is a Roman colony. We spent several days in that city. On the Sabbath day we went out beyond the gate, beside a river, where we thought there might be a place of prayer. We took a seat and spoke to the women who had come together. A woman named Lydia was listening, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God. The Lord opened her heart to heed what Paul was saying. After she and her household had been baptized, she pressed us to accept her offer: “If you are satisfied that I am faithful to the Lord, come into my home and stay.” And she would not take no for an answer.

A slave girl with a spirit of Python

Once, on our way to the place of prayer, a slave girl came to meet us who had a soothsaying spirit. Her fortune-telling brought in a large income for her masters. She trailed after Paul and the rest of us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, and they are announcing to you a way of salvation!” She kept this up for many days. In the end Paul grew weary and vexed. He turned and told the spirit, “I order you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that same hour.

Her masters saw that their hope of gain had gone out of her along with the spirit. So they laid hold of Paul and Silas and hauled them off to the rulers in the marketplace. Bringing them before the magistrates, they said, “These men are upsetting our whole city. They are Jews, and they preach customs that we cannot lawfully take up or follow, since we are Romans.” The crowd too rose up against them, and the magistrates tore the clothes off them and ordered them beaten with rods. When they had struck them many blows, they threw them into prison and told the jailer to keep them safely locked up. Given such a charge, the jailer threw them into the inner part of the prison and made their feet fast in the stocks.

Midnight in the prison at Philippi

At midnight, as Paul and Silas prayed, they sang praises to God, and the prisoners listened. All at once a great earthquake struck, so strong that the prison was shaken to its foundations. In that instant all the doors came open, and the chains of every prisoner fell loose. Startled out of sleep, the jailer saw that the prison doors stood open. Believing that the prisoners had got away, he drew his sword, ready to take his own life. But Paul shouted at the top of his voice, “Do not hurt yourself! Every one of us is still here!” He called for lights and ran inside, and shaking with fear he fell at the feet of Paul and Silas. He led them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” They answered, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” And they shared the word of the Lord with him and with everyone in his household. Even at that hour of the night he took them and bathed their wounds, and straightaway he was baptized together with all his family. Leading them up into his house, he spread a table for them, and the whole household rejoiced with him, now that he had believed in God.

Roman citizens released

In the morning the magistrates sent their lictors with the order, “Let those men go.” The jailer passed the message on to Paul: “The magistrates have sent orders for your release. So come out now, and go in peace.” But Paul told them, “We are Roman citizens, and they beat us in front of everyone without condemning us in any court, and threw us into prison. Are they now going to send us away in secret? Certainly not! Let them come in person and lead us out.” The lictors carried these words back to the magistrates, who were frightened to hear that the men were Roman citizens. They came and pleaded with them, and after leading them out, they kept asking them to leave the city. So they came out of the prison and went to Lydia. They saw the brothers and sisters and encouraged them, and then they set out.

fields.title: Acts 17
fields.body_html:
Reasoning from the Scriptures in Thessalonica

They traveled on through Amphipolis and Apollonia and came to Thessalonica, where the Jews had a synagogue. As he usually did, Paul went to the synagogue, and on three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, opening them up and laying out the case that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. “This Jesus I am proclaiming to you,” he said, “is the Christ.” Some of the Jews were convinced and threw in their lot with Paul and Silas, as did a large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few of the city’s leading women. But the Jews grew jealous. They rounded up some troublemakers from the marketplace, gathered a mob and threw the city into an uproar. They stormed Jason’s house, looking for Paul and Silas to bring them out before the people. When they could not find them, they hauled Jason and some of the brothers and sisters before the city officials, shouting, “These men who have stirred up trouble all over the world have now come here, and Jason has taken them into his home! They all defy Caesar’s decrees and say there is another king, one called Jesus.” Hearing this, the crowd and the city officials were thrown into alarm. They made Jason and the others post a bond, and then let them go.

Berea examines the Scriptures

That same night the brothers and sisters lost no time in sending Paul and Silas off to Berea. When they got there, they went to the Jewish synagogue. The Jews here were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica. They took in the message with real eagerness and went through the Scriptures day after day to check whether what Paul said was true. So many of them believed, along with a good number of Greek women of standing, and of men as well. But when the Jews of Thessalonica found out that Paul was proclaiming the word of God in Berea as well, they came there too, unsettling the crowds and stirring up trouble. At once the brothers and sisters sent Paul off toward the coast, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind. The men escorting Paul took him all the way to Athens. Then they set off back with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as they could.

A city full of idols

While Paul waited for them in Athens, he was deeply troubled in spirit to see the city crowded with idols. So he argued in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearing Gentiles, and every day in the marketplace with anyone who happened to come by. Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also took him on in debate. Some of them said, “What is this scrap-collector of ideas trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be promoting foreign gods.” They said this because he was announcing the good news about Jesus and the resurrection. They took him and brought him before the Areopagus. “May we know,” they said, “what this new teaching of yours is? Some of the things we hear from you sound strange to us, and we would like to know what they mean.” (All the Athenians, and the foreigners who lived there, spent their leisure on nothing but telling or hearing the latest new idea.)

To an unknown god

Paul stood up in front of the Areopagus and said: “People of Athens, I can see that in every respect you are extremely religious. As I walked around and looked closely at the things you worship, I even came upon an altar with this inscription: ‘To an unknown god.’ So what you worship without knowing it, I now make known to you. God, who made the world and all that is in it, is himself Lord of heaven and earth. He does not dwell in shrines that hands have made. Nor do human hands wait on him as if he lacked anything, since it is he who gives life and breath and all things to everyone. From one ancestor he made every nation of humankind to live over the whole face of the earth. He fixed the times set for them and the bounds of the places where they would live, so that they would seek God and perhaps grope their way toward him and find him. And yet he is not far away from any of us. It is in him that we live and move and exist. As some of your own poets have also put it, ‘We too are his offspring.’ If we are God’s offspring, then, we must not suppose that the divine nature resembles gold, silver or stone, carved into shape by human art and invention. God has passed over those times of ignorance, but now he orders people everywhere, all of them, to repent, because he has fixed a day on which he is going to judge the world in righteousness through a man he has appointed. And he has given everyone a pledge of this by raising him from the dead.”

When they heard about the raising of the dead, some scoffed, while others said, “We will listen to you on this another time.” With that, Paul went out from among them. But some people attached themselves to him and believed. Among them were Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus council, a woman called Damaris, and others besides.

fields.title: Acts 18
fields.body_html:
Paul comes to Corinth

After this, Paul left Athens and went on to Corinth. There he met a Jew called Aquila, born in Pontus, who had lately arrived from Italy with his wife Priscilla, since Claudius had ordered every Jew to leave Rome. Paul went to see them, and because he and they worked at the same craft, he stayed in their home and worked with them. By trade they were tentmakers. Each Sabbath he debated in the synagogue, seeking to win over Jews and Greeks alike.

A year and a half in Corinth

Once Silas and Timothy had come down from Macedonia, Paul gave himself fully to the word, bearing witness to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. But they set themselves against him and spoke abusively, so he shook out his clothes and said to them, “Your blood is on your own heads. I am clear of it. From now on I am going to the Gentiles.” Paul left them and went over to the home of a man named Titius Justus, who worshiped God. His house stood right beside the synagogue. Crispus, who led the synagogue, believed in the Lord, and so did everyone in his household. Many other people in Corinth heard the message, believed and were baptized. In a vision at night the Lord told Paul, “Stop being afraid. Go on speaking, and do not fall silent. I am with you. No one will lay a hand on you to hurt you, because many in this city belong to me.” Paul stayed on for eighteen months, teaching the word of God among them. But while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews joined forces against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat. Their charge was this: “He is talking people into worshiping God in a way the law does not allow.” Paul was about to speak when Gallio said to the Jews, “If this were some wrong or a serious crime, you Jews, I would have good reason to take up your case. But these are disputes over teaching and titles and your own law. Deal with them yourselves. I will not sit in judgment on matters like these.” Then he had them driven away from the judgment seat. Then they all grabbed Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But Gallio paid no attention to any of it.

Back to Antioch, and Apollos in Ephesus

Paul remained many days longer. Then he took leave of the brothers and sisters and sailed for Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila went with him. In Cenchreae he had his head shaved, since he had made a vow. They arrived at Ephesus, where Paul was to leave Priscilla and Aquila. He went into the synagogue on his own and debated with the Jews. They urged him to stay longer, but he would not agree. As he said goodbye, he told them, “I will come back to you, if God wills,” and he put out to sea from Ephesus. He came ashore at Caesarea, went up to greet the church, and then went down to Antioch. After some time there he set out again and journeyed through the Galatian country and Phrygia, town after town, building up all the disciples. A Jew called Apollos, born in Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was a gifted speaker and could handle the Scriptures with power. He had been taught the way of the Lord, and with great zeal he spoke and taught the facts about Jesus correctly, though the only baptism he knew was John’s. He started to speak out fearlessly in the synagogue. Priscilla and Aquila heard him there, and they took him in and taught him the way of God more precisely. Apollos planned to go across to Achaia, and the brothers and sisters encouraged him in it. They wrote to the disciples there, asking them to welcome him. Once he came, he gave much help to those who had come to believe through grace, for he argued powerfully and publicly against the Jews, proving them wrong, and used the Scriptures to show that Jesus is the Christ.

fields.title: Acts 19
fields.body_html:
Disciples who knew only John’s baptism

While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul made his way through the inland regions and came down to Ephesus. There he came upon some disciples and asked them, “When you came to believe, did you receive the Holy Spirit?” They told him, “No. We never even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.” Paul asked, “Then into what were you baptized?” “Into John’s baptism,” they answered. Paul said, “The baptism John performed marked people’s repentance, and he told the people to believe in the one who would come after him, namely Jesus.” When they heard this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. Then as Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them. They began speaking in tongues and prophesying. In all, the men numbered about twelve.

Two years in the hall of Tyrannus

Paul went into the synagogue, and for three months he spoke there without fear, debating and trying to win people over about the kingdom of God. Some, though, hardened themselves and refused to be persuaded, and they spoke against the Way in front of the gathering. Paul then withdrew from them, taking the disciples apart with him, and each day he held discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. This carried on for two years, with the result that all the people of the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord.

The sons of Sceva and the books of magic

God worked miracles of no common kind through Paul’s hands, so that people would even take cloths and work aprons that had touched his skin to those who were ill. Their sicknesses left them, and the evil spirits came out. There were also some Jewish exorcists who traveled from town to town, and they tried calling on the name of the Lord Jesus over people who had evil spirits. “I charge you by the Jesus whom Paul preaches,” they would say. A Jewish high priest named Sceva had seven sons who were doing this. The evil spirit answered them, “I know Jesus, and I am acquainted with Paul. But you, who are you?” Then the man who had the evil spirit threw himself on them. He mastered every one of them and was too strong for them, so that they fled from that house stripped of their clothes and covered with wounds. Everyone in Ephesus, Jews and Greeks alike, came to hear of this. Fear took hold of them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was more and more honored. Many who had believed began coming forward to confess and to disclose their practices. A good number of those who had practiced magic collected their books and burned them where everyone could see. When the value of the books was added up, it came to 50,000 silver coins. So with great power the word of the Lord kept growing and gaining strength.

After these events, Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go on to Jerusalem. “Once I have been there,” he said, “I must see Rome as well.” Paul sent Timothy and Erastus, two of the men who assisted him, on to Macedonia, but he remained in the province of Asia for some time longer.

Great is Artemis of the Ephesians

Around that time a serious uproar broke out over the Way. There was a silversmith named Demetrius who made silver shrines of Artemis, and he provided plenty of work for the craftsmen. He gathered them, and the workers in trades like theirs, and told them, “Men, you know well that our wealth comes from this work. You also see and hear what this Paul is doing. Not only in Ephesus, but across nearly the whole of Asia, he has won over a large crowd and drawn them away by telling them that anything made with hands is no god. It is not only that our trade risks being despised. The temple of the great goddess Artemis may come to count for nothing, and she, the goddess whom all Asia and the whole world worship, may soon be pulled down from her greatness.”

On hearing this they flew into a rage, and they kept shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” Confusion spread through the city, and with one impulse the people stormed into the theater, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, the Macedonians who traveled with Paul. Paul was ready to go in and face the assembled people, but the disciples kept him from doing so. Some of the Asiarchs, too, who were his friends, sent word to him and pleaded with him not to put himself at risk in the theater. Meanwhile people shouted all kinds of things, some one thing and some another. The assembly was in chaos, and most of them had no idea what had brought them there. Some of the crowd told Alexander what to say, since the Jews had pushed him forward, and Alexander signaled with his hand, intending to speak in his own defense to the people. But as soon as they realized he was a Jew, they all joined in one shout, and for about two hours they cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” The town clerk managed to quiet the crowd and said, “People of Ephesus, is there anyone at all who does not know that this city of the Ephesians has been entrusted with the temple of the great Artemis and with the image that fell from heaven? No one can dispute these facts, so you ought to keep calm and not do anything reckless. These men you have dragged here are not temple robbers, and they have not insulted our goddess. So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a case against anyone, there are court days and there are proconsuls; let the parties bring their charges against each other there. Any further matter you raise will be dealt with in the lawful assembly. Indeed, today’s events put us in danger of being accused of rebellion. There is no cause we could point to, nothing we could say to explain this disorderly gathering.” With these words he sent the assembly away.

fields.title: Acts 20
fields.body_html:
Through Macedonia and Greece

When the uproar had died down, Paul sent for the disciples and encouraged them. Then he said goodbye and set out for Macedonia. He went through those parts, speaking at length to the disciples to encourage them, and came to Greece. He stayed there three months. Just as he was about to sail for Syria, the Jews laid a plot against him, so he made up his mind to go back through Macedonia. He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus from the province of Asia. These men went on ahead and waited for us at Troas. We ourselves sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and five days later we joined them at Troas. We spent seven days there.

Eutychus at Troas

On the first day of the week we met together to break bread. Paul spoke with the people there, because he intended to leave the next day, and his talk went on until midnight. There were plenty of lamps in the upstairs room where we had gathered. A young man named Eutychus sat in the window opening. Paul’s talk ran longer and longer, and Eutychus sank into a heavy sleep. Overcome by it, he fell from the third floor to the ground, and when they lifted him up he was dead. Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and held him close. “Do not be upset,” he said, “his life is in him.” Then he went back upstairs, broke the bread and ate. He went on talking with them a long time, until dawn, and then he left. They led the boy away alive, and they were greatly comforted.

From Troas to Miletus

We went on ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, where we meant to take Paul on board. He had arranged it this way, because he wanted to go there on foot. When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went on to Mitylene. We sailed from there and the next day arrived off Chios. The day after that we crossed to Samos, and a day later we reached Miletus. Paul had decided to sail on past Ephesus so as not to lose time in the province of Asia. He was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if he could, by the day of Pentecost.

Paul speaks to the elders of Ephesus

From Miletus he sent word to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. When they had come, he said to them, “From the first day I set foot in the province of Asia, you have seen what kind of life I led among you the whole time. I worked as the Lord’s servant, with all humility and with tears, enduring the trials that the plots of the Jews brought on me. You know how I held back nothing that was for your good, but made it known to you and taught you, in public and from house to house. To Jews and Greeks alike I bore solemn witness about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus. And now, bound by the Spirit, I am on my way to Jerusalem. What I will meet there I do not know, except that in one city after another the Holy Spirit bears witness to me that chains and hardships lie ahead of me. But I set no value on my life, as if it were precious to me. All I want is to run my course to the end and carry out the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus: to bear full witness to the gospel of the grace of God.

And now I know this: you will not see my face again, not one of you among whom I have gone from place to place proclaiming the kingdom. So on this day I solemnly tell you: I am free from guilt for anyone’s blood. I never drew back from making known to you God’s whole plan. Be on your guard, for yourselves and for the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers to shepherd the church of God, which he won for himself through his own blood. Once I have gone, I know, savage wolves will force their way in among you, with no mercy for the flock. And from your own ranks people will stand up and speak twisted things, to lure the disciples into following them. So be watchful, and remember: for three years I did not stop, night or day, admonishing each one of you with tears. And now I place you in the care of God and of the message of his grace. That message has power to build you up and to give you your share among all who have been made holy. I never set my heart on anyone’s silver or gold or clothing. You know yourselves that I provided for my own needs, and for those who were with me, with these hands. In every way I set you an example: by working hard like this we must come to the aid of the weak, and keep in mind the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”

Farewell at Miletus

After saying this, he knelt down and prayed with them all. They all wept freely. They threw their arms around Paul and kissed him again and again. Above all, they were pained by what he had said, that they would not see his face any more. Then they went with him down to the ship.

fields.title: Acts 21
fields.body_html:
The voyage to Tyre

When we had parted from them, hard as it was, and put out to sea, we made a straight run to Cos. The next day we came to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. There we found a ship bound across the sea for Phoenicia, so we went aboard and put out. We came in sight of Cyprus and passed it by on our left, sailing on toward Syria, and we put in at Tyre, because the ship was to discharge its cargo there. We looked up the disciples there and stayed seven days. Speaking through the Spirit, they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. When our time there came to an end, we set out on our way again. The whole company, wives and children too, walked with us until we were outside the city. On the shore we went down on our knees and prayed, and we took leave of one another. Then we boarded the ship, and they went back to their homes.

In the house of Philip at Caesarea

We brought the voyage from Tyre to its end at Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers and sisters and spent a day with them. The next day we left and came to Caesarea. We made our way to the house of Philip the evangelist, who had been one of the seven, and stayed as his guests. Philip had four daughters who were not married, and they prophesied. During our stay of several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. He came to us, took Paul’s belt, and bound his own feet and hands with it. He said, “Here is what the Holy Spirit says: ‘Like this the Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man this belt belongs to, and they will give him up into the hands of the Gentiles.’” At these words, we ourselves joined the people of the place in urging Paul again and again not to go up to Jerusalem. Paul replied, “What do you mean by weeping and crushing my heart? For my part, I am prepared to be bound in Jerusalem, and more than that, to die there, for the name of the Lord Jesus.” Since he would not be persuaded, we said no more except, “Let the Lord’s will be done.”

After those days we got our things ready and set out on the road up to Jerusalem. Some of the disciples from Caesarea came along with us. They took us to the house of Mnason, a man of Cyprus and a disciple from the early days, so that we could stay with him.

Paul with James and the elders

When we came to Jerusalem, the brothers and sisters were glad to welcome us. On the day after, Paul took us with him to James, and the elders all came. After greeting them, Paul told them, item by item, everything God had accomplished among the Gentiles through the service he had been given. On hearing this they glorified God, and they said to Paul, “Look, brother, at the tens of thousands of believers there are among the Jews, and every one of them is deeply devoted to the law. Yet word has reached them that you are teaching the Jews scattered among the Gentiles to abandon Moses, and that you say they should no longer circumcise their children or follow the customs. So what is to be done? There is no doubt they will hear that you have arrived. Here is our advice, then. Four men among us have taken a vow on themselves. Bring these men with you, be purified along with them, and cover the cost of their offerings so that they can shave their heads. Then everyone will see that the reports about you are empty, and that you yourself live in line with the law and keep it. For the Gentiles who have come to believe, we have already written what we decided: they are to avoid meat sacrificed to idols, and blood, and anything strangled, and sexual immorality.” Then Paul took the men along. On the following day he was purified with them and went into the temple, announcing when their days of purification would be over and the offering for each of them would be presented.

Seized in the temple

The seven days were nearly over when some Jews from Asia caught sight of Paul in the temple. They threw the whole crowd into confusion and laid hands on him, shouting, “People of Israel, help! This is the man whose teaching, everywhere he goes, sets everyone against our people, the law and this place. And now he has even brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place unclean.” For they had seen Paul in the city a little earlier with Trophimus, a man of Ephesus, and they took it for granted that Paul had taken him into the temple. The entire city was set in motion, and the people rushed together. They laid hold of Paul and hauled him out of the temple, and straightaway the gates were closed. They were set on killing him when a report went up to the tribune in command of the cohort that the whole of Jerusalem was in turmoil. He immediately took soldiers and centurions and rushed down on the crowd, and at the sight of the tribune and the soldiers they left off beating Paul. Coming up to Paul, the tribune took him into custody and gave orders to fasten him with two chains. He began asking who the man was and what he had been doing. But the crowd shouted back, some one thing, some another. The din made it impossible for him to get at the facts, so he had Paul taken into the barracks. At the stairs, the crowd’s violence was such that the soldiers had to carry Paul up. The whole mass of people came after them, crying out, “Away with him!”

Paul asks to speak to the people

As they were about to take him into the barracks, Paul said to the tribune, “May I have a word with you?” The tribune said, “You know Greek? So you are not the Egyptian who stirred up a rebellion a while ago and led the 4,000 men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?” Paul answered, “I am a Jew, a man of Tarsus in Cilicia, and a citizen of a city of some note. I ask you, allow me to address the people.” The tribune gave permission, and Paul, standing on the steps, raised his hand to the people. When all had fallen silent, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language. He said:

fields.title: Acts 22
fields.body_html:
Paul’s defense to the people of Jerusalem

“Brothers and fathers, listen now to the defense I am making before you.”

When they heard him speaking to them in Hebrew, they grew even quieter. Then he went on: “I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia but raised here in this city. I sat at the feet of Gamaliel and was trained with great precision in our ancestral law. I was as zealous for God as every one of you is today. I persecuted this Way to the point of death, putting men and women alike in chains and handing them over to prison. The high priest himself can confirm this, and so can the whole council of elders. I even got letters from them to our fellow Jews in Damascus, and I set off to bring the people there back to Jerusalem in chains to be punished.

A light from heaven near Damascus

As I was traveling and coming close to Damascus, at about midday, all at once a brilliant light from heaven blazed around me. I dropped to the ground and heard a voice say to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?’ ‘Who are you, Lord?’ I answered. He told me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, the one you are persecuting.’ My companions saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one who was speaking to me. I asked, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ The Lord answered, ‘Get up and go on into Damascus. There you will be told all that has been assigned for you to do.’ Because the glory of that light had left me unable to see, my companions led me by the hand, and I came into Damascus. There was a man named Ananias, devout in keeping the law and well regarded by all the Jews who lived there. He came and stood beside me and said, ‘Brother Saul, see again!’ In that very moment my sight came back, and I looked up at him. Then he said, ‘The God of our ancestors has chosen you beforehand to know his will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear words from his own mouth. You will be his witness to everyone, telling what you have seen and heard. Now why wait any longer? Get up and be baptized. Let your sins be washed away as you call on his name.’

A trance in the temple

After I had come back to Jerusalem, I was praying in the temple when I fell into a trance. I saw the Lord, and he said to me, ‘Hurry! Leave Jerusalem at once, for the people here will not accept what you tell them about me.’ I answered, ‘Lord, these people know well what I did. In one synagogue after another I had those who believe in you locked up and beaten. When Stephen, your witness, was put to death and his blood poured out, I was there myself. I agreed with what they did, and I looked after the cloaks of those who killed him.’ Then he told me, ‘Go! I am going to send you far away, to the Gentiles.’”

A Roman citizen by birth

The crowd heard him out until he said this. Then they raised a shout: “Take a man like this off the face of the earth! He should never have been allowed to live!” They kept yelling, flinging off their cloaks and tossing dust into the air. So the tribune ordered Paul taken into the barracks. He gave orders for him to be questioned under the whip, to find out why the people were shouting at him so. They had stretched him out and tied him with straps when Paul said to the centurion on duty, “Does the law allow you to flog a Roman citizen, and one who has had no trial?” When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and told him, “What is this you are about to do? This man is a Roman citizen!” The tribune came over and asked him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” “Yes,” he said. The tribune replied, “It cost me a great deal of money to get this citizenship.” Paul answered, “And I am one by birth.” At once the men who were going to question him backed away. The tribune, too, grew afraid once he learned that Paul was a Roman citizen, since he had had him tied up.

Brought before the council

On the following day, since the tribune wanted to learn the true reason for the charges the Jews were bringing against Paul, he freed him from his chains. He summoned the chief priests and the full council, then brought Paul down and placed him in front of them.

fields.title: Acts 23
fields.body_html:
Paul before the council

Paul fixed his eyes on the council and said, “Brothers, I have conducted my life before God with a fully clear conscience up to this very day.” At that, Ananias the high priest told the men standing near Paul to hit him in the mouth. Then Paul said to him, “God will strike you in turn, you whitewashed wall! You are seated to try me by the law, and you break that same law by having me hit?” Those standing by said, “You insult God’s own high priest?” Paul answered, “Brothers, I was not aware that he was the high priest. For Scripture says, ‘Never speak ill of one who rules your people.’”

Aware that the council was made up partly of Sadducees and partly of Pharisees, Paul called out to them, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, born to a family of Pharisees. It is over the hope of the dead rising that I am on trial.” As soon as he said this, the Pharisees and Sadducees began to quarrel, and the gathering split in two. The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, and neither angel nor spirit, but the Pharisees hold to both, the resurrection and the world of spirits. The shouting grew loud, and some experts in the law from the Pharisees’ party got to their feet and fought the point: “We see no fault in this man. And if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him, what then?” The dispute became so fierce that the tribune feared Paul would be pulled apart between them. He told the troops to go down, seize Paul out of the middle of them, and take him into the barracks.

Take courage

The following night the Lord came and stood beside Paul. “Take courage,” he said. “Just as you have borne witness to me in Jerusalem, you must bear witness in Rome as well.”

More than forty men under a curse

When day came, a group of Jews banded together and swore an oath, calling down a curse on themselves if they ate or drank anything before they had killed Paul. More than forty men took part in this plot. They went to the chief priests and the elders and told them, “We have put ourselves under a solemn curse: we will not taste a thing until we have killed Paul. So now you and the council must tell the tribune to bring Paul down to you, claiming that you want to look into his case more closely. We will be waiting to kill him before he ever reaches you.”

But Paul’s nephew, the son of his sister, got word of the ambush. He made his way into the barracks and warned Paul. Paul called over one of the centurions and said, “Bring this young man to the tribune; he has news for him.” The centurion brought him to the tribune and reported, “The prisoner Paul called me over and asked me to take this young man to you, since he has a message for you.” The tribune took hold of his hand, led him off to one side by themselves, and asked him, “What is this news you have for me?” He answered, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as if the council meant to look more carefully into his case. Do not let them persuade you. More than forty of their men are lying in wait for him. They have sworn under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed him, and they are ready now, only waiting for you to say yes.” The tribune sent the young man away with a warning: “Do not let anyone know you told me about this.”

Sent by night to Felix the governor

Then he summoned two of his centurions and told them, “Have 200 soldiers ready to leave for Caesarea at nine o’clock tonight, with seventy horsemen and 200 spearmen.” He also had them provide mounts for Paul to ride, so that he would reach Felix the governor safely. And he wrote a letter that went like this: “Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent Governor Felix: greetings. The Jews had taken hold of this man and were on the verge of killing him. I came on the scene with the troops and pulled him out of their hands, having found out that he was a Roman citizen. Since I wanted to learn the grounds of their charges against him, I had him brought before their council. I found he was being accused over points of their own law, but with nothing that called for death or chains. Word reached me that a plot was being laid against him, so I am sending him to you straight away, and I have told his accusers to state their case against him in your presence.”

The soldiers followed their instructions: they took charge of Paul and marched him through the night to Antipatris. The next day they left the horsemen to go on with him and went back to the barracks themselves. When the horsemen reached Caesarea, they handed the letter to the governor and brought Paul before him as well. After reading the letter, the governor asked what province Paul belonged to, and learned that it was Cilicia. “I will give you a full hearing,” he said, “once your accusers are here as well.” Then he gave orders for Paul to be held under guard in Herod’s praetorium.

fields.title: Acts 24
fields.body_html:
Tertullus brings the case against Paul

Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some of the elders and a trained advocate named Tertullus, and they laid out their case against Paul before the governor. When Paul had been called in, Tertullus opened the prosecution: “Thanks to you we live in great peace, and your careful planning has set many things right for this nation. Most excellent Felix, we welcome all this in every way and in every place, with heartfelt thanks. But I do not want to keep you long, so I ask you, in your fairness, to give us a brief hearing. This man, we have found, is a public menace. He causes unrest among the Jews in every part of the world, and he is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even attempted to defile the temple, and we took hold of him. Question him yourself, and you will learn from him all about the things we accuse him of.” The Jews who had come added their voices, claiming that it was all so.

Paul makes his defense before Felix

The governor signaled to Paul to speak, and he answered: “You have judged this nation for many years, and knowing that, I am glad to answer for myself before you. It is only twelve days, no more, since I went up to Jerusalem to worship, as you can find out. They never found me in the temple in debate with anyone or drawing a crowd together, nor in the synagogues, nor anywhere in the city. They have no proof to set before you for the things they now charge me with. This much I do acknowledge before you: it is as one who follows the Way, which they call a sect, that I serve the God of our ancestors. I believe all that accords with the law and all that stands written in the Prophets. My hope rests on God, and these men look for it too: that a resurrection is coming, of the righteous and the unrighteous alike. That is why I, for my part, take pains to live with a blameless conscience toward God and toward people at all times. I had been away for a number of years, and I came to bring charitable gifts to my people and to make offerings. I was doing this when they found me in the temple, ritually purified, with no crowd around me and no disorder. But some Jews from Asia were the ones who saw me. They should have come before you to accuse me, if they have any complaint against me. Otherwise, let the men who are here tell you what wrong they discovered in me when I stood before the council, unless it was the one sentence I called out as I stood among them: ‘I am being judged by you today over the resurrection of the dead.’”

Felix knew a good deal about the Way, and he postponed the matter. He told them, “I will rule on your case once Lysias the tribune comes down.” He gave orders to the centurion: Paul was to stay in custody, but with some relief from strict confinement, and none of his own people were to be kept from helping him.

Felix and Drusilla hear Paul

A few days afterward Felix arrived with Drusilla, his wife, a Jewish woman. He had Paul brought in and heard what he had to say about faith in Christ Jesus. As Paul reasoned with him about righteousness, self-control and the judgment that is coming, Felix became alarmed. “Leave me for now,” he answered. “I will call for you again when I find a suitable time.” At the same time he hoped for money from Paul, so he had him brought in quite often and talked with him.

Two full years went by, and then Porcius Festus succeeded Felix. Felix wished to earn the favor of the Jews, so he left Paul behind in chains.

fields.title: Acts 25
fields.body_html:
Festus hears Paul, and Paul appeals to Caesar

Festus had been in his province only three days when he left Caesarea and went up to Jerusalem. The chief priests and the most prominent Jews laid their charges against Paul before him and kept pressing him. They asked him for a favor that would harm Paul: to send for him to come to Jerusalem. They meant to lie in wait and kill him on the way. Festus replied that Paul was being held at Caesarea, and that he himself would soon be going back there. “So let your leading men travel down with me,” he said, “and if there is anything improper about this man, they can accuse him there.”

He spent no more than eight or ten days with them and then went down to Caesarea. The day after he arrived, he took his place on the judgment seat and had Paul brought in. As soon as Paul appeared, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem crowded around him and laid many heavy charges on him, none of which they could prove. Paul’s defense was this: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar.” Festus, though, was looking to build up favor with the Jews. He turned to Paul and said, “Would you agree to go up to Jerusalem and have these matters judged there, with me presiding?” Paul said, “The court I stand before is Caesar’s, and here is where my case belongs. I have wronged the Jews in nothing, and you know this quite well yourself. If I am guilty and have done something for which I deserve to die, I do not ask to be spared death. But if there is nothing in what these men accuse me of, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar!” Then Festus talked it over with his advisers and replied, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.”

Festus lays Paul’s case before King Agrippa

After some days had gone by, King Agrippa and Bernice came to Caesarea on a visit of welcome to Festus. Their visit lasted many days, and during it Festus told the king about Paul. “Felix left a certain man behind in custody,” he said. “When I went to Jerusalem, the chief priests and the Jewish elders laid information against him and asked me to condemn him. I told them that it is not the Roman way to give anyone up as a favor until the accused person has met the accusers face to face and been given a chance to answer the charge. So when they had come here with me, I lost no time. The very next day I took my place on the judgment seat and had the man brought in. His accusers stood up, but the charges they brought were not the crimes I had been expecting. What they had against him were certain questions about their own religion, and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul asserted to be alive. I was unsure how to go about investigating questions like these, and so I asked whether he would like to go to Jerusalem and have the matter judged there. But Paul appealed to be held for the emperor’s decision, so I ordered him to be kept in custody until I can send him on to Caesar.” Agrippa told Festus, “I have been wanting to hear the man for myself.”

“You will hear him tomorrow,” Festus replied.

So the following day Agrippa and Bernice came with a great show of splendor. They went into the hall of hearing along with the tribunes and the city’s most important men, and Festus gave the order for Paul to be brought. Then Festus spoke: “King Agrippa, and all of you who are here with us, look at this man. The entire Jewish people has come to me about him, in Jerusalem and here too, shouting that he has no right to go on living. I, for my part, saw that he had committed no crime that merits death. And as he has made an appeal to the emperor himself, I resolved to send him on. Yet I have nothing solid to put in a letter about him to my lord. That is why I have brought him out here before you all, King Agrippa, you above all, so that once he has been examined I may have something I can write. For to send a prisoner and not make clear what he is charged with seems senseless to me.”

fields.title: Acts 26
fields.body_html:
Paul makes his defense before Agrippa

Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak on your own behalf.” So Paul held out his hand and began to make his defense: “King Agrippa, I count myself fortunate that it is before you that I am to answer today for all the charges some Jews bring against me, especially as you know well all the customs and disputed questions of the Jews. So I ask you to hear me out with patience.

All Jews know how I have lived from my youth, from the very start of my life among my own people and in Jerusalem. They have known me a long time, and if they were willing they could testify that I lived as a Pharisee, in the strictest sect of our religion. And now I stand on trial because of my hope in the promise God made to our ancestors. It is the promise our twelve tribes hope to see fulfilled as they worship God with devotion night and day. It is for this hope, Your Majesty, that I am accused by Jews. Why do any of you think it unbelievable that God raises the dead? I myself was once convinced that I had to do all I could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth, and that is what I did in Jerusalem. With authority from the chief priests I shut up many of God’s holy people in prison, and when they were condemned to die, I cast my vote against them. Again and again I had them punished in all the synagogues and tried to force them to blaspheme. My rage against them knew no bounds, and I hunted them down even in cities beyond our land.

A light from heaven on the road to Damascus

That was my mission when I was on my way to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At noon, Your Majesty, as I traveled along the road, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, blazing around me and the men traveling with me. We all fell to the ground, and I heard a voice speaking to me in Hebrew: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It hurts you to kick against the goads.’ I asked, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ The Lord answered, ‘I am Jesus, the one you are persecuting. But rise, stand up on your feet. I have shown myself to you for a purpose: to choose you as my assistant and my witness, to tell what you have seen of me and what I will yet show you of me. I will keep you safe from your own people and from the Gentiles. I am sending you to them to open their eyes, so that they turn from darkness to light and from Satan’s power to God, and so receive forgiveness of their sins and a share in the inheritance among those sanctified by faith in me.’

And so, King Agrippa, I did not resist the heavenly vision. I went first to the people of Damascus, then to Jerusalem and the whole country of Judea, and to the Gentiles too, and I told them all to repent and turn to God, and to live in a way that proves their repentance. It was for this that some Jews seized me in the temple and set about murdering me. God has helped me, and up to this very day I stand here bearing witness to people of low and high rank alike. I say only what the prophets and Moses foretold: that the Christ must suffer, and that, as the first to rise from the dead, he would announce light both to our own people and to the Gentiles.”

Festus interrupts, and Paul appeals to the king

As Paul was saying this in his defense, Festus called out loudly, “You are out of your mind, Paul! All your great learning is pushing you into madness.” “I am not mad, most excellent Festus,” Paul replied. “The words I am speaking are truth and sound sense. The king understands these matters, and that is why I can speak to him so openly. I am sure that nothing of this has passed him by. After all, it did not happen in some out-of-the-way corner. King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe them.” Agrippa said to Paul, “In so short a time you are persuading me to become a Christian!” Paul answered, “Whether it takes little or much, my prayer to God is that not you alone but every one of my hearers today would come to be as I am, though without these chains.”

Nothing deserving death or chains

Then the king stood up, with the governor, Bernice and those seated with them. After they had gone out, they said to each other, “Nothing this man does calls for death or prison.” Agrippa told Festus, “This man might have gone free, had he not appealed to Caesar.”

fields.title: Acts 27
fields.body_html:
Paul sails for Italy

Once our voyage to Italy had been decided, they placed Paul and a number of other prisoners in the custody of Julius, a centurion of the Augustan cohort. We went aboard a ship from Adramyttium that was due to call at ports along the coast of Asia, and we put out to sea. Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, was with us. The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius was considerate toward Paul and allowed him to go to his friends and be looked after by them. Putting out from there, we sailed on the sheltered side of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. We crossed the open water off Cilicia and Pamphylia and came to Myra in Lycia. At Myra the centurion came across an Alexandrian ship headed for Italy and transferred us to it. For many days we made slow headway and only with difficulty arrived off Cnidus. Since the wind would not let us hold our course, we sailed in the shelter of Crete, passing Salmone. Working our way along the shore with difficulty, we reached a place called Fair Havens, close to the town of Lasea.

A great deal of time had gone by, and sailing was now hazardous, since even the Fast was past. So Paul gave them advice. “Men,” he said, “I can tell that this voyage is heading for harm and heavy loss, not only to the cargo and the ship but to our own lives too.” But the centurion put more trust in the helmsman and the owner of the ship than in what Paul was saying. The harbor was a poor place to spend the winter, so most of them were for putting out to sea again, in the hope of somehow getting to Phoenix to winter there. Phoenix is a harbor in Crete that faces both southwest and northwest.

The wind called Euraquilo

When a light breeze came up from the south, they thought their plan could be carried out. So they raised anchor and sailed along Crete, close to shore. But soon afterward a storm wind called Euraquilo, the northeaster, came rushing down off Crete. The ship was caught up in it and could not be turned into the wind, so we gave way and drifted before it. We ran in the lee of a small island called Cauda, and there, with great effort, we managed to secure the ship’s boat. After hoisting it aboard, the crew used ropes to brace the ship, passing them around the hull. They were afraid of being driven onto the sandbanks of the Syrtis, so they let down the sea anchor and were carried along in that way. The storm pounded us so fiercely that on the following day they started jettisoning the cargo. On the third day they took the ship’s spare gear and hurled it into the sea with their own hands. Day after day there was no sun and no stars to be seen, and the storm kept bearing down on us with great force. In the end every hope that we would come through alive was slipping away from us.

Take heart

No one had eaten for a long time. Then Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have heeded me and stayed in Crete instead of setting out. You would have avoided all this damage and loss. Even so, I now urge you to take heart. Not one life among you will be lost; only the ship will go. For during this night an angel came and stood beside me, an angel of the God whose I am and whom I worship. He told me, ‘Paul, do not be afraid. You are to appear before Caesar. And look: God has granted you everyone who is on board with you.’ So take heart, men! I believe God: it will happen just the way I was told. But we have to be cast ashore on some island.”

It was the fourteenth night, and we were drifting this way and that across the sea of Adria. Around midnight the crew started to suspect that land was coming near. They dropped a sounding line and found the water 120 feet deep. A little farther on they sounded again and found it 90 feet. They were afraid we might strike a rocky coast somewhere, so they threw out four anchors from the stern and prayed for morning to come. Meanwhile the sailors were trying to abandon the ship. They had lowered the boat into the sea on the excuse that they were about to run out anchors from the bow. But Paul told the centurion and the soldiers, “If these men do not stay on board, there is no way for you to be saved.” So the soldiers slashed the ropes of the boat and let it go.

Bread before daybreak

While they waited for daybreak, Paul kept encouraging all of them to take some food. “This is the fourteenth day,” he said, “that you have kept watch without eating, taking nothing at all. So I urge you to take some food. It is for your own survival, since not a hair on the head of any of you will be lost.” When he had said this, Paul took bread and, with everyone watching, thanked God for it. Then he broke it and started eating. Everyone was cheered by this, and they too took some food. There were 276 of us on the ship in all. Once everyone had eaten enough, they threw the wheat overboard to lighten the ship.

All brought safely to land

At daybreak the land was unfamiliar to them. But they caught sight of an inlet with a beach, and they made up their minds to drive the ship onto it if possible. They slipped the anchors and let them go into the sea, and at the same time they freed the lashings on the steering oars. Then they set the small front sail to catch the wind and steered toward the beach. But they came upon a place where two seas met and ran the vessel aground. Its bow dug in and held, unable to move, while the stern began to break apart under the violence of the waves. The soldiers meant to kill the prisoners, so that none of them could swim off and get away. The centurion, however, was determined to bring Paul through alive, and he held them back from what they meant to do. He told everyone who could swim to throw themselves into the sea first and head for the shore, and the rest to come after them, some on boards and others on wreckage from the ship. So it was that all of them came safely to land.

fields.title: Acts 28
fields.body_html:
Paul and the viper on Malta

Once we were safely ashore, we found out that the island was called Malta. The local people treated us with remarkable kindness. Because it had started to rain and it was cold, they lit a fire and made all of us welcome. Paul collected an armful of sticks and laid them on the fire. The heat brought out a viper, which clamped onto his hand. When the local people saw the creature dangling from his hand, they said to one another, “This man is surely a murderer. He came safely out of the sea, yet Justice will not let him live.” But Paul shook the creature off into the fire and was not harmed at all. They kept waiting for him to swell up or suddenly drop dead. After a long wait, when they saw that nothing strange was happening to him, they changed their view and began to say that he was a god.

Healing on the estate of Publius

Near that spot there was an estate that belonged to the leading man of the island, whose name was Publius. He took us in and treated us as his guests for three days. The father of Publius lay ill with bouts of fever and dysentery. Paul visited him, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him. After that, the rest of the island’s sick people kept coming to him, and they were healed. They heaped honors on us, and when the time came to sail, they loaded the ship with what we needed.

From Malta to Rome

Three months later we set sail on a ship from Alexandria that had spent the winter at the island. Its figurehead was the Twin Brothers. We landed at Syracuse and spent three days there. From there we weighed anchor and came to Rhegium. After one day a wind sprang up from the south, and on the second day we made Puteoli. There we found some brothers and sisters, who begged us to spend seven days with them. And that is how we came to Rome. The brothers and sisters there had heard about us, and they came out as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of them Paul gave thanks to God and took heart.

Once we were in Rome, Paul was given permission to live in private quarters, though a soldier guarded him.

Paul speaks with the Jewish leaders in Rome

Three days later Paul called together the leaders of the Jews. When they had gathered, he said to them, “Brothers, I have not acted against our people or against the customs of our ancestors. Even so, I was made a prisoner in Jerusalem and delivered into Roman hands. The Romans questioned me and were ready to let me go, since no charge against me called for death. But when the Jewish leaders there objected, I had no choice but to appeal to Caesar. I did this, not because I had any charge to bring against my own people. This is the reason I invited you here, to see you and speak with you: I wear this chain for the sake of Israel’s hope.” They answered him, “No letters about you have reached us from Judea, and none of our fellow Jews who have arrived here has brought word of anything against you. But we think it fair to hear your own views. What we do know about this sect is that it meets opposition everywhere.”

They fixed a day with him, and on it a larger group came to his lodging. From morning to evening he laid things out for them, bearing full witness to the kingdom of God and seeking to convince them about Jesus from the law of Moses and the Prophets. His words won some of them over, but others refused to believe. Divided among themselves, they began to go, but first Paul said one thing more: “How right the Holy Spirit was when he spoke to your ancestors through Isaiah the prophet, saying, ‘Go to this people and tell them, “You will listen and listen but never understand. You will look and look but never see. For the heart of this people has grown dull. Their ears are slow to hear, and they have shut their eyes, for fear that they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.”‘ Know this, then: this salvation from God has been sent to the Gentiles. They will listen.”

Two years in Rome, unhindered

For two full years Paul lived in lodgings he rented, receiving everyone who visited him. There he proclaimed the kingdom of God and taught the things about the Lord Jesus Christ, with all boldness, unhindered.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Know this, then: this salvation from God has been sent to the Gentiles. They will listen.”

— Acts 28:28

The last scene of Acts is a conversation in a rented room in Rome. Paul has called the leaders of the city’s Jewish community, and from morning to evening he lays out for them the kingdom of God and the things about Jesus, from the law of Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded; others refuse. Paul quotes Isaiah, as Jesus did, on a people who listen and never understand, and then announces that God’s salvation has been sent to the Gentiles. It is not a door shut on Israel. Paul goes on welcoming “everyone who visited him”, and the story ends with the door open.

The question the book leaves with you

On the day of Pentecost, when Peter had finished preaching, his hearers asked a question that echoes through the whole book:

These words pierced their hearts. They asked Peter and the rest of the apostles, “What are we to do, brothers?”

— Acts 2:37

A jailer in Philippi asks it at midnight, shaking, after an earthquake has thrown open the prison doors: “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” Paul gives an answer that echoes Peter’s call to repent and be baptized, and that the whole book gives: “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” Acts is full of people hearing the message and deciding what to do with it: three thousand at Pentecost, a eunuch in his chariot, a centurion and his household, a businesswoman named Lydia whose heart the Lord opened, philosophers in Athens who scoff or ask to hear more another time. King Agrippa, after listening to Paul’s defence, says half in mockery, “In so short a time you are persuading me to become a Christian!” Paul answers that he prays that everyone who hears him would become as he is, “though without these chains.”

Acts asks its readers the same question. Its message has reached us across nineteen centuries. What are we to do?

Where the book points

It points, first, to the Spirit. The disciples could do nothing until they had received power from on high, and nothing in Acts is done without him: the Spirit fills, sends, guides, forbids, and speaks to the church at prayer. Christians have differed on how the Spirit’s gifts in Acts are to be sought and expected today. But no reader of the book can doubt that the church lives by the Spirit or not at all.

It points, second, to witness. The last thing Jesus said before he was taken up was that his followers would be his witnesses to the farthest end of the earth. Acts tells how that began; it does not tell how it ends, because it has not ended. The book leaves Paul in Rome, and the rest of the journey to the ends of the earth to those who come after.

And it points to the church: a community devoted to the apostles’ teaching, the shared life, the breaking of bread and the prayers; Jews and Gentiles at one table; a people who quarrel and forgive, suffer and rejoice, and keep telling what they have seen and heard.

Where to go from here

Many writings in this library preach from Acts or continue its story. A few places to begin:

  • On the Holy Spirit. The second volume of A. B. Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, with its chapters on waiting for the Spirit and the outpouring at Pentecost; R. A. Torrey’s Baptism with the Holy Spirit, a classic statement of one view of the gift; and A. W. Tozer’s All with One Accord (2:1).
  • On the first preaching. Tozer’s The Triumph of the Resurrection (2:22–39), J. C. Ryle’s Only One Way (4:12), and Catherine Booth’s Witnessing for Christ (1:8; 5:32).
  • On the life of the first church. Devoted to Prayer, on how the first Christians prayed, from the upper room to Paul and Silas singing at midnight; and Andrew Murray’s The Holy Spirit and Money, on Ananias and Sapphira (5:3).
  • On Paul’s conversion (chapter 9). Charles H. Spurgeon’s Paul’s First Prayer (9:11).
  • On the jailer’s question (chapter 16). D. L. Moody’s The Way of Salvation (16:23–40) and R. A. Torrey’s The Way of Salvation Made as Plain as Day (16:30–31).
  • On Agrippa (chapter 26). John Wesley’s The Almost Christian (26:28).
  • On what happened next. Clement of Rome’s The First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, written from the church in Rome a generation later, which remembers Peter and Paul as witnesses who suffered to the end; and Eusebius of Caesarea’s The Church History, the first history of the church, which picks up the story where Acts leaves off.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Acts in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

But the best next step may be to read Acts again with Paul’s letters open beside it, and then to read the Gospel of Luke again, knowing how its story continues. And remember, as you close the book, the words two men in white spoke to the apostles as they stood staring into the sky. They were not to stay gazing, but to wait for the promise and then be witnesses. The one they had watched go would come again:

This Jesus has been taken up from you into heaven, and he will come in the very way you saw him leave for heaven.”

— Acts 1:11
